output:
*Interview with Bastien Girard, établisseur, of Le Locle, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Monsieur Girard, thank you for waiting. I am asking each of you about the evening, in order. Take your time.

GIRARD: My time is the one thing I have plenty of tonight, Inspector. Ask.

MATTHEY: Begin at dinner.

GIRARD: The master asked us to show him our watches, as he does every year. I would not. He would only have told me what was wrong with mine in front of his wife and his nephew, and I have had enough of Aurèle Monnier telling me things.

MATTHEY: You had a disagreement with him that evening.

GIRARD: About the price of his repeater. I buy movements and parts and I put my firm's name on what I sell, and I wanted the rights to the watch he had been four years on. I offered what I thought it was worth. He thought it was worth more. We did not come to an agreement.

MATTHEY: After dinner, where did you go?

GIRARD: I sat on alone in the dining room with the brandy. I heard the temple strike ten there. I did not look at my watch.

MATTHEY: And then?

GIRARD: I went out into the street to smoke, at twenty-one minutes past ten by my watch, and I stayed under the front windows of the house. It was cold, Inspector. Hard frost, and old snow on the kerb. I walk in the cold when I want to think, and I smoke Brissago, the cheap ones. A man who is owed money cannot afford better.

MATTHEY: Who owes you money?

GIRARD: Félix Monnier. He knows it, and he has avoided me. I don't say that to make trouble. It is a fact of business.

MATTHEY: What did you hear from the house?

GIRARD: The piano started up in the salon just as I lit my cigar, at twenty-nine minutes past ten by my watch. I don't know music. I know a piano when I hear one.

MATTHEY: Did you hear anything else?

GIRARD: At twenty-six minutes to eleven by my watch I heard faint quick bells from the master's window up above. I did not know what they were.

MATTHEY: You are sure of the time?

GIRARD: I am sure of my watch. A merchant notices time, Inspector. It is how he keeps his money.

MATTHEY: What did you do then?

GIRARD: I came back into the house at fourteen minutes to eleven by my watch. The hall clock had just struck eleven and its face showed two minutes past eleven. I went straight up to Félix in the library.

MATTHEY: Why did you go to him?

GIRARD: To ask him for my money.

MATTHEY: You have spoken of Dr Vauthier at dinner. What is your opinion of him?

GIRARD: He is a pleasant man at table, if you like cigars and Latin tags. I do not like his company. He is always very sure that he is the cleverest man in any room, and he is usually right, which does not help.

MATTHEY: Thank you, Monsieur. That is all for now. Please do not leave the house until I have spoken to the others.

GIRARD: I have no wish to leave it, Inspector. It is a cold night, and I have a warm bed waiting.
